t: A military junta is rule by a committee of officers, usually installed by a coup; it differs from a military strongman, who rules alone, and from civilian governments that merely depend on the army.
Korea’s Goryeo generals ruled collectively from 1170, but juntas became common only after 1945, governing much of Latin America, Africa and Asia and, for shorter spells, Greece, Turkey and Portugal.
Juntas usually promised to restore order and then hold elections; many did hand power back, but many also imprisoned, tortured and killed opponents, and one coup often led to another.
dyk: Junta, Spanish for “meeting” or “council”, won its political fame through the committees Spaniards formed in 1808 to resist Napoleon’s invasion; these were not military councils, and the word only later came to mean rule by officers.
ev: Goryeo’s generals seize power in Korea and rule through their council while kings reign as figureheads
Soldiers expel England’s Rump Parliament; army officers draft a constitution making Oliver Cromwell Lord Protector
Spaniards form local and national juntas to resist Napoleon’s invasion, the councils from which the modern term derives
Colonels seize power in Greece and rule until their coup in Cyprus brings their fall in 1974
The commanders of Chile’s army, navy, air force and police seize power and rule as a junta until 1990
Ethiopia’s military council, the Derg, deposes Emperor Haile Selassie and rules until 1987
Argentina’s armed forces seize power; defeat in the Falklands War of 1982 forces them to hold elections in 1983
Myanmar’s armed forces seize power in a coup on 1 February, their third takeover since 1958

f.power: A committee of senior officers, usually the commanders of the army, navy and air force and sometimes the police, ruling by decree
f.legitimacy: A claim to rescue the nation from disorder, corruption or subversion, resting on control of the armed forces and often on a promise of later elections
f.chosen: Officers take power by coup and fill the council by rank; members change through internal manoeuvres or counter-coups, and juntas end by handing over to civilians or being overthrown
f.examples: The Goryeo military regime in Korea (1170–1270), the Greek military junta (1967–1974), the Chilean Government Junta (1973–1990), the Derg in Ethiopia (1974–1987), Argentina’s National Reorganization Process (1976–1983), Myanmar’s State Law and Order Restoration Council (1988–1997)
